article.summary: Four games, two models, three independent generations per condition. Astra identifies 12/12 correctly; DeepSeek identifies 7/12.

article.intro: We replicate the weight-reading experiments in Weight-Space Programming, beginning with a direct question: what can a trained network’s weights reveal about its purpose?
article.experiment_title: Can a model identify a game just by reading the network’s weights?
article.method: We use the four released PPO policies, all with identical input channels, action spaces and network dimensions. Each model receives the 17,253 weights as text and the architecture description, with no candidate game names and no tools. Astra and DeepSeek each make three independent attempts.
article.table_caption: Each cell lists independent runs 1 / 2 / 3. ✓ Correct; ✕ incorrect.
article.takeaway: Astra gets all three attempts right for every game. DeepSeek does so only for Breakout. With correct=1 and incorrect=0, DeepSeek’s other three tasks each have a sample variance of 0.3333 across generations; Astra’s four tasks each have variance 0.
article.no_js: The interactive card requires JavaScript. All classification results are available in the table below.
article.card_caption: Switch games, models and repeats to inspect the actual answers. Replays are from the original authors; classifications are from our replication.
article.grading_note: Scoring uses game categories: a Frogger-style road-crossing answer is accepted for Freeway. Confidence is self-reported; output token counts include reasoning tokens.
article.error_analysis: DeepSeek’s five errors are three Sokoban guesses, one Snake guess and one Asterix guess. In the first Pac-Man attempt, it reconstructs a symmetric maze from the weights but names Asterix with 88% confidence. Recovering spatial structure and identifying the game are distinct steps.
